So gaunt against the gibbous moon, Piercing the silence velvet-piled, A lone wolf howls his ancient rune— The fell arch-spirit of the Wild.

1
🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Clauses, and the two ways a sentence goes wrong
Professor Lovelore At the board
0:50
An AI-generated character and voice.
Clause
A group of words with a subject and a verb.
What is being said about the subject? That is the verb.
Who or what does it? That is the subject.
Independent clause
It can stand alone as a sentence.
Perrault built a fire.
Dependent clause
It starts with a word like when, because, although, or after, and it leans on the rest.
When the ice broke.
Complex sentence
One of each. Dependent clause first, comma after it.
When the ice broke, Perrault built a fire.
Fragment: too little
A dependent clause left on its own.
When the ice broke.
Run-on: too much
Two independent clauses jammed together with nothing between them, or with only a comma.
The ice broke Perrault built a fire.
2
✏️ Grammar: Learn the Labels
Step 1 of 4 this week: label a sentence.
TermWhat it isExample
independent clausehas a subject and a verb and can stand alonePerrault built a fire.
dependent clausehas a subject and a verb but starts with a joining word and cannot stand aloneWhen the ice broke
subordinating conjunctionthe joining word that starts a dependent clause: when, because, although, after, while, if, since, until, asWhen the ice broke
complex sentenceone independent clause and at least one dependent clauseWhen the ice broke, Perrault built a fire.
fragmenttoo little: often a dependent clause left aloneBecause the ice broke.
run-ontoo much: two independent clauses with nothing between them. With only a comma, it is a comma splice.The ice broke, Perrault built a fire.

Pick a label, then tap the part it belongs to. Tapping any word inside a clause labels the clause.

Because Buck’s feet had grown soft,
François made him four moccasins.
🔁 Same facts, other order
Buck limped all day because his feet had grown soft.

When the independent clause comes first, the comma usually goes away. When the dependent clause comes first, the comma stays.

🪶 Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, Mimic
One sentence from Chapter III, three ways.
“Hungry as he was, he would not move to receive his ration of fish, which François had to bring to him.”Jack London · The Call of the Wild, Chapter III
📖 Read like a Reader

What does this sentence show about Buck’s feet, and about what François does for him?

✏️ Read like a Writer

London opens with Hungry as he was, and the refusal comes after the comma. What does that order do to the way you read the rest? Then look at how the sentence ends.

🖊️ Mimic

Write a sentence about someone else that opens the same way, then holds the surprise for the middle and ends with what another person has to do.

___ as he was, he would not ___, which ___ had to ___.

📖 Priya’s draft, a model
Priya
7th Grade Scholar · Buck at the last fight

Priya changed her line after reading the whole chapter.

In Chapter III, Buck stops fighting fair and starts fighting to win. When the chapter begins, he is still a dog who stays out of trouble. By the last fight, that dog is gone. When Spitz is beaten, London writes, “There was no hope for him. Buck was inexorable” (Ch. 3). Inexorable means nothing can turn him aside. Not even a beaten enemy. Because Buck shows no mercy, I think he has lost the fairness he had at Judge Miller’s place. The North made him stronger, but it took away the fair and trusting kind of dog he used to be.
